Sooty antbird (Hafferia fortis) neonates emerge at a remarkably modest mass, with freshly hatched chicks weighing just 4.8 grams [Wwb = 4.8 grams] in the humid lowland forests of western Amazonia. This initial body mass, measured from broods in undisturbed terra firme, underscores the altricial condition typical of thamnophilid antbirds, where hatchlings are nearly naked and entirely dependent on biparental provisioning. The eggs themselves incubate over a period averaging 13 days [ab = 13 days], though this embryonic development proceeds most efficiently under the stable thermal conditions of a well-maintained nest, where internal temperatures cluster around 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Field observations from long-term studies in Ecuador suggest that slight deviations from this incubation temperature can delay hatching or reduce chick viability. Once hatched, the nestlings undergo rapid feather development and somatic growth, fuelled by a diet of arthropods delivered by both parents, a strategy that minimizes the time spent vulnerable to predators in the understory.

The altricial nestlings reach the critical stage of fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and departure from the nest, at 13 days after hatching [tx = 13 days after hatching] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This brief nestling period is fairly typical for a passerine of this body size and reflects the intense predation pressure common in Neotropical forest understories, where nests face high rates of loss to snakes and mammals. Comparatively, the age at fledging is shorter than that reported for some larger-bodied congeners in the same subfamily, possibly linked to the species’ relatively modest ultimate adult mass. The transition to independence follows shortly after nest departure, with juveniles associating with adults for several additional weeks while refining foraging skills on ants and other leaf-litter arthropods.

This relatively rapid gonadal development is notable for an understory insectivore that must compete for territories in a saturated environment. However, the first successful breeding event is significantly deferred relative to the attainment of physical maturity. The ultimate adult wet weight of the sooty antbird stabilizes at about 35 grams [Wwi = about 35 grams], placing it among the medium-sized members of the Thamnophilidae. This asymptotic mass is achieved gradually over the first several months of life, with juveniles approaching adult dimensions well before their first breeding season. The species exhibits only modest sexual dimorphism in body mass, with males averaging slightly heavier than females, though the overall range overlaps considerably. Body composition analyses from mist-netted individuals in southeastern Peru indicate that this adult wet weight of about 35 grams [Wwi = about 35 grams] is maintained across the year with little seasonal fluctuation, reflecting the relatively stable arthropod prey base available in lowland Amazonian forests. Achieving a body mass of around 35 grams [Wwi = around 35 grams] is consistent with the species’ foraging ecology as a terrestrial and understory gleaner, a niche that favors maneuverability over raw power.

Reproductive output in the sooty antbird is characterized by a conservative strategy typical of many long-lived tropical passerines. Breeding pairs typically attempt a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], although renesting may occur following a predation event during the incubation or nestling phase. A fixed two-egg clutch [N_R_i = two-egg clutch] and a single annual clutch [F_R_i = single annual clutch] reflect a life-history strategy prioritized toward adult survival rather than maximizing annual fecundity.
